channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: The Triumph of Barry Mackenzie
item.description: Barry Humphries' comic-strip ocker hero Barry Mackenzie is being made into a film by director Phillip Adams and actor Barry Crocker, with backing from the Australian Film Development Corporation, and the production marks a turning point for an Australian film industry finally willing to celebrate its own vulgar traditions.

item.title: Victoria, Bring Back the Lash
item.description: Victoria remains one of the few places on earth that still has judicial flogging on its statute books, and Keith Dunstan examines the public debate after Judge Gillard and the Victorian Bar warn that courts risk being seen as too lenient on violent offenders.

item.title: Melbourne Keeps Its 'Hair' On
item.description: A report on opening night of the musical 'Hair' at Melbourne's Metro Theatre, where the audience dressed as gurus and swamis outnumbered ordinary patrons, Ron Barassi attended in the front row, and Harry Miller's post-show mystery buses toured the city before arriving at a whitewashed Fitzroy dairy showing Judy Garland films and Carmen Miranda.

item.title: Will the Man in the Abstract Painting Be the Model of the Year?
item.description: A Suave menswear fashion parade at the Savoy Plaza Hotel presents the 1971 look, a riot of knickerbockers, hot pants for men, burgundy shirts and striped overalls, leading Keith Dunstan to stand alone in anxiously awaiting the resurgence of blue serge.

item.title: How the Pure Sunday Disappeared in Melbourne
item.description: The 1971 Melbourne Sunday newspaper wars, in which the Sunday Observer folds and is replaced almost overnight by the Melbourne Observer under Max Newton, leaving readers hunting half a dozen milk bars to assemble a complete cover, and the managing director of the Sunday Review cautiously optimistic about the quarter million Melburnians who will still buy Sunday papers.

item.title: What Next to Expect from Sex
item.description: A survey of the sex creeping into Melbourne's comic strips, fairy tales, Collins Book Depot's bestseller lists, and even the rejuvenated Sexton Blake detective series, concluding that the day cannot be far off before someone publishes a sex book by Malcolm Muggeridge.

item.title: Shandy: a Menace or a Mockery?
item.description: Cooper's Brewery launches a two percent alcohol shandy in a gold ring-top can, prompting outrage from church groups, stern warnings from school mothers' clubs, and the alarming prospect that Carlton and United might buy up milk bars all over the country and give them mock-Tudor fronts.

item.title: Wrong Bishop Wronged
item.description: A letter from M. E. Ryan of St Kilda correcting Batman's Melbourne of 20 March 1971, which misidentified Bishop Phelan as the administrator of the Melbourne diocese in 1921, explaining that the Very Reverend John Barry held that role, and that Phelan had severed his connection with the archdiocese in 1913.

item.title: The Woeful Fat Man Says It's a Glorious Climate
item.description: Melbourne's notorious weather, which wrecked an entire Test Match and drew comment from Robert Menzies, inspires a dossier of celebrated complaints reaching back to 1863, from Ellen Kean to Marcus Clarke's 'Glorious Climate' monologue.

item.title: The Pharters on the Hill Know the Game's Lovely Ritual Qualities
item.description: A defence of Test cricket's solemn ritual against calls to brighten it up, arguing that its magnificent, unalterable dullness is its greatest charm, drawing on statistics from W. L. Murdoch in 1881 and a comparison with Chinese Opera as evidence that nothing has ever really happened and nothing ever will.

item.title: Give the Disreputable Flag to the Pentridge Graduate, Said Phelan
item.description: The history of Melbourne's St Patrick's Day processions, from the triumphs of Archbishop Mannix and his fourteen Victoria Cross winners in 1920 to the 1971 edition, which has been reduced to a Summer Happening at the Myer Music Bowl with proceeds to the Yooralla School.

item.title: Would the Young Males Step Forward, Please?
item.description: With Australia apparently devoting a quarter of its female population under 21 to beauty contests, Keith Dunstan wonders why charities have entirely overlooked young males as contestants, who are surely equally deserving of trips around the world, dream automatic sedans, and free hairdos.

item.title: Alexandra the Great Says It's Hard for a Real Exotic Dancer
item.description: For Moomba, Ferdinand Nemeth's club El Toro Espana in Russell Street has imported Alexandra the Great, billed as possessing the world's biggest bust, and Keith Dunstan goes backstage to talk with the St. Louis-born Geraldine Paredes about the decline of proper exotic dancing in an era when a girl who will take off all her clothes straight off the street is considered sufficient.

item.title: Marriage A La Mode — Spanish, Medieval or Oz
item.description: Melbourne's wedding reception industry is booming, with the city's new registry office installed in the Bullion Room of the old Treasury Building and Governor Rohan Delacombe opening Chaucer's, a $750,000 medieval-themed reception complex on Canterbury Road, complete with kosher kitchen, cantilever lavatories and parking for 160 cars in what the owners might reasonably call Arthur's Stables.

item.title: You Don't Have to Go to Adelaide to Be Corrupted
item.description: Keith Dunstan argues that Melbourne's strip and nudity entertainment scene, from lunchtime shows at El Toro Espana to theatrical productions at Her Majesty's and the Chevron, can match anything Adelaide is marketing as its 'Oh! Calcutta!' coach tours, and that Melbourne's puritan reputation is undeserved.

item.title: The SF World of Bems, Sercons and BNFs
item.description: Science fiction is experiencing its greatest boom after years of near-irrelevance, with Melbourne hosting two SF conventions in 1971, mounting a bid for the 1975 World Science Fiction Convention, and opening Australia's first dedicated SF bookshop, Space Age Books on Swanston Street, run by Mervyn Binns.

item.title: When All is Revealed There's Nothing New Left to See
item.description: The annual cat-and-mouse game between General Motors-Holden and Australia's press reaches its peak with the launch of the new HQ Holden, described through elaborate factory security, undercover photography at the Dandenong plant, and the spectacular stunt of dangling the new models from BHP-ESSO helicopters over Bass Strait for a TV commercial.

item.title: What a Sporty Way to Govern a Country
item.description: Exasperated by the newspaper eulogies for departing political leaders, Keith Dunstan proposes an all-sport Australian Cabinet, with Don Bradman as Prime Minister, Ron Barassi as his deputy, Ron Clarke as Treasurer, Jack Dyer handling industrial relations, Keith Miller for Transport, and Peter Thomson for National Development.

item.title: With a Tear in His Eye He Said Goodbye
item.description: The end of the 1971 Victorian Football League season brings the simultaneous retirement of Ron Barassi from Carlton and the resignation of Bobby Rose from Collingwood, prompting wall-to-wall press coverage and intense speculation about the coaching vacancy at Collingwood, whose traditions Keith Dunstan compares with the Japanese code of the Samurai.

item.title: Breaking Down Sexual Apartheid in a Most Endearing Way
item.description: Geelong Grammar School headmaster T. R. Garnett announces the admission of girls from first term 1972, prompting Keith Dunstan to recall the fierce gender segregation of his own public school days and speculate on the transformation the change will bring to Corio's bleak landscape.

item.title: Will Howling Ruffians and Unsexed Women Threaten Melbourne Again?
item.description: The Victorian Government's moves to extend late-night shopping hours provoke a debate about the character of Melbourne's city centre after dark, drawing on Victorian-era warnings about howling ruffians and unsexed women to argue that fears about deregulated shopping hours are as overblown now as they were a century ago.

item.title: The Very Hard Week That Was
item.description: A report on Melbourne Wine Week, centred on a grand tasting at the Two Faces restaurant, with notes on the calibre of South Australian entries, the heroic endurance required of serious wine judges, and the state of the Australian wine industry as it faces a bottling boom from South Australia.

item.title: Now It's Hard to Be Caught with a Kids' Movie
item.description: A report on a Warner Brothers breakfast screening of a new film, where the Melbourne cinema circuit has adopted the American practice of pre-release breakfasts for press and buyers, and where the line between children's and adult films has become impossible to hold in the age of R-rated blockbusters.

item.title: The Beautiful Square Dream
item.description: A look at the long-delayed plans for Melbourne's City Square, surveying the proposals that have come and gone over 115 years and the latest design by the Theosophy Society, while questioning whether the square, once built, will become a genuinely beautiful civic space or merely a windy concrete plaza.

item.title: Whatever Is Happening to Toorak
item.description: A lament for the decline of old Toorak, as wreckers demolish its mock Tudor streetscape to make way for a Safeway supermarket and office tower called the Village Centre.

item.title: Breakfasting with the Stars, the South Yarra Push and Tails
item.description: A tour of the Melbourne Cup carnival season, from pre-race breakfasts at Flemington to the South Yarra social set in their tail-coats, with observations on the strange Melbourne tradition of morning champagne and the contest between formal dress and the new informality.

item.title: How to Be a Stylish Gold Digger Without Getting Your Feet Muddy
item.description: A tour of Victoria's competing goldfield tourist towns, from Wedderburn's fossicking pond to Ballarat's Sovereign Hill historical park, where the gold is purchased from a bank and the dunny wall is already growing honeysuckle.

item.title: Doing My Way on an Old Cigar-Box Lid
item.description: A visit to Rosalind Humphries' exhibition of paintings on cigar-box lids, which reprises a celebrated 1969 Buxton's Galleries show, while a parliamentary row over the appointment of former ASIO officer Michael Thwaites as Commonwealth Parliamentary Librarian raises questions of political discrimination in the public service.

item.title: Getting Gorton Back with Kisses, Meetings and an Old Shoe Box
item.description: A report on the grassroots Melbourne campaign to restore John Gorton to the Liberal leadership, including meetings at Malvern Town Hall, a shoe-box petition drive, and the view from a PR man that Gorton's charisma and public sympathy could yet make him Prime Minister again.

item.title: Now Here's a Dame Who Slept Around
item.description: A lament for four Melbourne institutions closing at once, the Oriental Hotel at the Paris end of Collins Street, the Regent Theatre with its Vintage Hoyts decor, the Tasma Guest House in Parliament Place, and Hilliers milk bar by the Regent, all falling to wreckers over the Christmas break.
